facts.text: The evidence does not support selecting stage gates, technology readiness levels, systems-engineering verification and validation planning, test and evaluation master plans, assumption-based planning or discovery-driven planning as a complete planning method.
facts.quote: The evidence does not support choosing one of stage gates, technology readiness levels, systems-engineering verification and validation planning, test and evaluation master plans, assumption-based planning or discovery-driven planning as the complete method.

facts.text: Treating the different planning methods as competing end-to-end methodologies risks building the wrong planning system.
facts.quote: Treating them as competing end-to-end methodologies is one of the easiest ways to build the wrong planning system.

facts.text: Commitment-control methods decide when an organization is allowed to continue; examples are Stage-Gate, GAO knowledge points, DOE Critical Decisions, Front-End Loading and the UK Gateway Review process.
facts.quote: Commitment-control methods (Stage-Gate, GAO knowledge points, DOE Critical Decisions, Front-End Loading, the UK Gateway Review process) decide when the organization is allowed to continue.

facts.text: Knowledge-measurement methods define readiness and what must be demonstrated with which data; examples are TRL and technology readiness assessment, simulation credibility scales, V&V planning and test-and-evaluation planning.
facts.quote: Knowledge-measurement methods (TRL and technology readiness assessment, simulation credibility scales, V&V and test-and-evaluation planning) define what "ready" means and what must be demonstrated with which data.

facts.text: Learning-under-uncertainty methods organize work around what is not yet known; examples are assumption-based planning, discovery-driven planning, hypothesis-driven experimentation, spiral development, set-based design and parallel paths.
facts.quote: Learning-under-uncertainty methods (assumption-based planning, discovery-driven planning, hypothesis-driven experimentation, spiral development, set-based design, parallel paths) organize the work around what is not yet known.

facts.text: Planning methods can be distinguished by six practical questions: governance asks when continuation is allowed; maturity asks whether technology is mature enough for the next use; evidence asks what must be demonstrated, how and with what test data; uncertainty asks what is assumed and what must be learned. Schedule asks how likely completion by the fixed date is, and communication asks whether reviewers can see the logic and gaps.
facts.quote: Six questions separate them in practice: governance (when may we continue?), maturity (is the technology mature enough for the next use?), evidence (what must be demonstrated, how, and with what test data?), uncertainty (what are we assuming and what must we learn?),

facts.text: A strong plan should use one method from each of the commitment-control, knowledge-measurement and learning-under-uncertainty families.

facts.text: No evidence supports a single best planning method.
